problem_markdown: For an integer $n>2$, let $V=\{1+kn:k\ge1\}$. Call an element irreducible if it is not a product of two elements of $V$. Prove that some element of $V$ has two different factorizations into irreducibles, ignoring factor order.
solutions_markdown:
Some prime divisor $p$ of $n-1$ is not congruent to one modulo $n$; otherwise their product $n-1$ would be congruent to one. Let $d\ge2$ be the multiplicative order of $p$ modulo $n$. Then $p^d$ is irreducible in $V$.

Choose $a>1$ with $pa\equiv1\pmod n$ and $p\nmid a$. Such an $a$ exists by varying an inverse of $p$ modulo $n$ through multiples of $n$. Factor $pa$ into irreducibles in $V$, which is possible by repeated splitting into smaller factors. Exactly one factor, say $m$, contains $p$, with exponent one.

The number $m^d$ has the factorization into $d$ copies of $m$. It also equals $p^d(m/p)^d$, where $(m/p)^d\in V$ because $m/p\equiv p^{-1}\pmod n$, and $m/p>1$. Factor that second factor into irreducibles. This new factorization contains $p^d$, which differs from $m$ by its $p$-exponent. The factorizations are distinct.
